title: Chiral Nonlinear Optics and Optical Control
authors: Cedric Dufresne, Annabelle Makowski, Nir Rotenberg
abstract: Chiral light-matter interactions lie at the heart of emerging technologies such as quantum network protocols and quantum logic gates. In the few photon regime, it has been shown that chiral interactions between photons and a waveguide-embedded two-level quantum emitter can break reciprocity and impart a directional $π$ phase shift while the transmission remains intact. In this work, we present a model for multicolor, chiral nonlinear interactions in waveguides using a Green's Tensor formalism. We challenge previously held notions and demonstrate the complex photon dynamics hidden in multicolor light-matter interactions in the few photon regime. By modulating a stronger control beam, we can manipulate a weaker signal beam that contains much less than a single photon per emitter lifetime, on average. We develop equations for the transmission of the signal photons and removing the control photons to uncover the true strength of these nonlinearities, which we show is stronger than what is possible in symmetric geometries. The model predicts tunable unity extinction and up to 30% amplification in the signal, a $\sim$100x increase from standard predictions in which control photons are present. We also predict a tunable 0-$π$ phase shift via control modulation with significant robustness to emitter imperfections. Our model opens a new regime of directional nonlinear quantum light-matter interactions for study, providing a route to efficient all-optical control of photons.
summary: This theoretical study models chiral nonlinear optics in waveguides using a two-level emitter coupled to multiple optical fields. By employing the Green's Tensor formalism, the authors show that chirality enables superior control over photon dynamics compared to symmetric setups. The results predict highly efficient all-optical switching and amplification crucial for quantum networking applications.
main_problem: The work investigates chiral nonlinear interactions between light (signal and control beams) and a quantum emitter in photonic waveguides to achieve all-optical control of photons.
main_result: Chiral geometries enable robust, tunable $0-\pi$ phase shifts and significantly enhance signal amplification ($\sim 100	imes$) compared to standard predictions.
method: The authors develop a model using the Green's Tensor formalism and solve the emitter dynamics via the Lindblad master equation in the rotating frame.
model_or_system: The system involves a two-level quantum emitter coupled to a waveguide, driven by both signal ($\omega_s$) and control ($\omega_c$) beams. The theory incorporates chirality through directional coupling parameters ($D$).
key_observables: Transmission ($T$), reflection ($R$), coherent transmission ($T_{	ext{coh}}$), and the phase shift of the transmitted signal beam.
important_parameters: Few-photon regime ($ ar{n}_c < 1$), chirality parameter ($D$), detunings ($\delta$), and Rabi frequencies ($\Omega_{s/c}^R$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on time averaging to remove oscillatory terms, and approximations are used for calculating relative population contributions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup comparing symmetric vs. chiral coupling; spectra show TLE interaction signatures in $T$ and $R$; other figures compare normalized transmission under different control powers.
paper_structure: The paper builds from first principles using a Green's Tensor formalism to model the Hamiltonian, derives equations of motion for the density matrix, calculates time-averaged observables like transmission, and finally compares results between symmetric and chiral geometries.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses quantum network protocols by demonstrating highly controllable, non-reciprocal nonlinear light-matter interactions necessary for advanced photonic quantum devices.

figures.caption: Figure 1. a) The TLE coupled to the waveguide interacting with the signal and control light fields. b) The ideal chiral case where only one mode will couple to the TLE, leading to directional emission. c) The ideal symmetric case where the TLE couples to both directions, leading to equal emission in either direction.

Figure 2. The transmission and reflection spectra when both the signal and control beams are interacting with the TLE. This is considering a perfect system with unity coupling and assuming no scattering losses or noise. Signatures of the TLE dressed state interaction can be observed at different signal- emitter detunings: three photon amplification is shown in red, energy transfer between the signal and control beams is shown in green, and the AC-Stark effect is shown in blue. These effects are discussed in more detail in Sec. IV B below.

Figure 3. Frequency dependence of T s norm and Rs norm for symmetric (a,b) and chiral (c,d) geometries. The control power is set to Ωc R = 3Γ and signal power Ωs R = 0.1Γ. The dashed blue line is the line cut plotted below in Fig. 4.

Figure 4. Line cut spectra of T s (solid), T s coh (dashed), and T s norm (dot dashed) with Ωc R = 3Γ, 5Γ, 7Γ (blue, purple, teal), ∆= 3Γ, and Ωs R = 0.1Γ for a) symmetric geometry and b) chiral geometry.

The control detuning is fixed (∆= 3Γ) and the con- trol power is swept Ωc R = 0Γ, 1Γ, 1.5Γ, 2Γ, 4Γ denoted by red, purple, teal, mint, and green respectively for weak signal Ωs R = 0.001Γ.
